overview: The exact atlas id shirvan maps a Shirvanshah state in the eastern Caucasus from 1000 to 1200, not the whole modern region or every community living there. The Persianized Yazidid or Kasranid dynasty ruled mainly from Shamakhi, sometimes using Baku, while negotiating with Darband, Arran, Georgian kingdoms, Rus raiders, Oghuz groups, and Seljuq overlords. Coins, a lost local history preserved through a later compilation, Persian court poetry, and neighboring chronicles illuminate rulers far better than ordinary households. The two atlas polygons each contain one ring and 37 decoded positions; sampled Shamakhi, Baku, Qabala, Aghsu, Mingachevir, and even an offshore Caspian point fall inside, proving the frontier is deliberately rough. People farmed, herded, fished, crafted, traded, studied, worshipped, raised children, treated illness, and managed waste with resources that varied sharply by place and status. Written-language sample: فلک کژروتر است از خط ترسا, Falak kazh-rawtar ast az khatt-e tarsa, meaning the heavens are more crooked than a Christian's script. Khaqani wrote this Persian verse in the twelfth-century Shirvan court world. At 1200 the software label ends, but the dynasty and regional life continued.

periods.title: 1000 to 1028: Yazid consolidates a Persianized court
periods.summary: Yazid ibn Ahmad ruled a state already rooted in an Arab-origin dynasty that had become culturally Persian. Coins and the later-preserved local history trace expansion around Layzan and neighboring districts. Shamakhi served as the main court center, while the atlas begins its exact Shirvan layer at 1000.

periods.title: 1028 to 1045: Manuchihr faces Rus attack and uncertainty
periods.summary: Persian royal names become prominent with Manuchihr. In 1030 Rus arriving from the Caspian landed near Baku, defeated his force, and moved toward Baylaqan. The episode reveals maritime danger and regional alliances, but surviving narrative comes through later transmission and leaves ordinary experiences mostly unrecorded.

periods.title: 1045 to 1067: walls, Oghuz pressure, and shifting rivals
periods.summary: A ruler named Qubad fortified Shamakhi with a stone wall and iron gates around 1045, a practical response to repeated danger. Oghuz movements, dynastic rivalry, and neighboring powers kept the lowlands exposed. A wall protected a city more plausibly than it defined every pasture or village.

periods.title: 1067 to 1094: Fariborz submits to Seljuq supremacy
periods.summary: Fariborz faced Qarategin's invasion and the wider advance of Alp Arslan. He accepted Seljuq overlordship and paid heavy tribute, while coins acknowledged greater rulers. Local kingship survived inside an imperial hierarchy, showing that vassalage could restrict sovereignty without erasing the court, population, or regional economy.

periods.title: 1094 to 1120: succession puzzles and Seljuq intervention
periods.summary: After Fariborz, ruler sequences become difficult to reconstruct because names, coins, and later chronicles do not align neatly. Seljuq power returned directly, and Sultan Mahmud occupied Shirvan early in the twelfth century. Political uncertainty at court did not make farms, workshops, ports, or families disappear.

periods.title: 1120 to 1160: Manuchihr III and Georgian connections
periods.summary: Manuchihr III rebuilt royal authority while Georgian power grew across the Caucasus. Marriage, warfare, protection, and rivalry tied the courts together. Persian poetry flourished at Shamakhi, where the ruler's title helped inspire Khaqani's pen name, though literary praise must never be mistaken for an audited government report.

periods.title: 1160 to 1191: Akhsitan, poetry, trade, and overlords
periods.summary: Akhsitan I patronized a court known through Khaqani and other literary voices while navigating Georgian and Ildegozid power. Baku's harbor, petroleum, fishing, and caravan links mattered increasingly. Coin chronology revises older ruler lists, reminding readers that even elegant dynastic timelines are assembled from stubborn fragments.

periods.title: 1191 to 1200: shocks, rivalry, and an atlas handoff
periods.summary: Late twelfth-century Shirvan faced Ildegozid pressure, competing princes, and a severe earthquake reported around 1191 or 1192. Sources disagree about details and immediate political effects. The atlas stops the exact id at 1200, although Shirvanshah lines, towns, families, languages, and economic networks continued afterward.

sections.title: Read the exact name, dates, and map

items.text: Exact id shirvan is an atlas record for a state ruled by Shirvanshahs, not a label for every historical land called Shirvan or every modern Azerbaijani ancestor. Its imported name is useful, but the public card must supply dynasty, period, and evidence boundaries.

The 1000 feature is one Polygon with one component, one ring, and 37 decoded positions. Its bounding box runs approximately from 46.85 to 50.47 degrees east and 39.48 to 41.18 degrees north. Those precise decimals describe software coordinates, not surveyed medieval border stones.

The 1100 feature also has one component, one ring, and 37 positions, but its coordinate hash differs slightly. Sampled Shamakhi, Baku, Qabala, Aghsu, and Mingachevir remain inside. Shaki, Quba, Salyan, Derbent, Ganja, Tbilisi, Ardabil, Dvin, Ani, and Alamut remain outside.

The exact feature is absent at 900, appears at 1000 and 1100, then disappears at 1200, 1279, and 1300. That tidy software span is not a founding ceremony or last battle. The Shirvanshah dynasty began earlier and survived for centuries after this card.

Coverage records confirm two intervals and two border files, while the card index, override file, and missing-card registry show no reviewed card before integration. All four review fields were pending. This packet therefore attaches only to exact id shirvan and creates no shared-content association.

The Shirvanshahs descended from an Arab military family established under Abbasid rule, yet their court became thoroughly Persianized. By this period rulers bore Persian names and titles. Identity changed through language, marriage, patronage, and local rule; it was not a simple replacement of one population by another.

Coins name rulers and sometimes overlords, mints, titles, and dates, making them unusually direct political evidence. They do not explain harvests, marriages, punishments, or jokes. A coin can settle part of a succession puzzle while remaining remarkably unhelpful about who cleaned the mint floor.

Modern specialists have revised Manuchihr III's and Akhsitan's chronology by comparing coins with literary genealogies. Several similarly named princes may have ruled overlapping districts. A clean family tree is tempting, but the evidence supports branches, co-rulers, and uncertainty rather than one effortless sequence.

Islamic coins joined royal protocol with pious formulas and often circulated in regional currency zones. Minting expressed authority, yet a local coin could acknowledge a caliph or sultan above the issuer. Money therefore records layered sovereignty more clearly than a modern flag-and-border model does.

The eastern Caucasus sat between Iranian, Armenian, Georgian, steppe, and Caspian worlds. Turkic-speaking Oghuz newcomers changed military and political life, while older languages and communities endured. Calling the period simply Persian, Arab, Turkic, or Caucasian hides the multilingual reality that rulers had to manage.

sections.title: Navigate neighbors, tribute, diplomacy, and war

items.text: Darband guarded the narrow Caspian passage north of Shirvan. Its Hashimid rulers, urban factions, religious warriors, and craft or professional groups could support or depose leaders. Shirvan's rulers fought, negotiated, and intermarried around this gate, whose politics were more crowded than a two-color map suggests.

The Shaddadids controlled parts of Arran, including Ganja and at times Ani, directly west of Shirvan. Rivalry, alliances, and pressure from larger powers connected their fortunes. A shared frontier did not prevent merchants, captives, soldiers, pilgrims, and news from crossing in both peaceful and frightening ways.

Seljuq expansion brought Shirvan into a broad imperial order. Fariborz paid tribute and acknowledged the sultan while retaining local rule. Tribute meant real extraction from resources and labor, even when chronicles discuss only rulers. Someone ultimately produced every dinar that made diplomatic submission look tidy on paper.

Seljuq succession struggles repeatedly weakened central control, allowing atabegs and local dynasties room to maneuver. Sultan Mahmud's intervention in Shirvan shows that autonomy changed with imperial strength. The polity was neither permanently independent nor merely a province; its rulers negotiated a moving hierarchy.

The Ildegozid atabegs became major powers in Azerbaijan during the later twelfth century. Shirvanshahs balanced their demands against Georgian connections and internal rivals. Court marriages, hostages, tribute, military help, and titles could all carry political weight, though surviving sources rarely reveal how villagers judged the arrangement.

sections.title: Walk Shamakhi, Baku, ports, and roads

items.text: Shamakhi was the main royal center, while Baku served as a Caspian port and later residence. Medieval writers noticed Baku's petroleum, natural harbor, fishing, shipping, and caravan connections. Oil was already useful and taxable, though nobody was commuting through medieval traffic in a petroleum-powered family car.

Caravans connected inland towns with Iranian and Caucasian markets, while ships crossed the Caspian. Merchants handled tolls, credit, weights, languages, weather, animals, and political permission. Long-distance commerce depended on local porters, stable workers, market sellers, translators, and guards, not only glamorous travelers.

Baku's walled urban landscape contains many layers, but its celebrated Shirvanshah Palace is mainly fifteenth century. The World Heritage listing helps explain the city's long importance while warning against moving every surviving tower, mosque, bath, or palace backward into Akhsitan's exact lifetime.

Heritage investigators read walls, street patterns, reused masonry, inscriptions, and restoration history together. Their work confirms a layered medieval city rather than one frozen construction date. For this card, Baku is a real port and residence, but individual monuments require their own dates before joining the family photograph.

Derbent's massive fortifications channeled travel between the Caucasus and Caspian coast. They provide regional comparison for defensive engineering, customs, garrisons, and urban life. Derbent was a neighboring polity, not automatically a Shirvan city, so its famous walls cannot substitute for missing Shamakhi buildings.

sections.title: Farm, herd, eat, craft, and trade

items.text: Across medieval Iran and the Caucasus, wheat and barley supported bread and porridge, while orchards, gardens, livestock, and irrigation diversified food. Exact Shirvan harvest tables do not survive. Weather, soil, warfare, taxes, and status shaped meals, so no single royal banquet represents a farming household.

The Kura and Aras lowlands and neighboring Mogan plain supported grazing, farming, and irrigation where water and security allowed. Channels required digging, clearing, allocation, and repair. A map can color the plain in seconds; keeping water moving through silt and arguments was considerably harder.

Later Shahsevan evidence documents seasonal movement between plains and mountain pastures, but it cannot be copied wholesale into twelfth-century Shirvan. It does show how mobile herding can leave thin written traces. This card treats pastoral movement as plausible regional context, not a timeless ethnic costume.

Water-buffalo remains at medieval Barda show animals and husbandry practices moving through the Islamic Caucasus. That evidence belongs to neighboring Arran, not every Shirvan village. It nevertheless expands the regional farmyard beyond horses and sheep and reminds us that political borders did not stop livestock knowledge.

Kashk, made from processed dairy or grain, could preserve nutrition for later use and appears in medical as well as culinary traditions. Bread, dairy, meat, fish, fruits, and vegetables varied by landscape and means. Preserved food was practical technology, especially when the pantry lacked refrigeration and optimism.

sections.title: Meet households, women, children, and social ranks

items.text: Elite women bearing the title khatun could possess dynastic rank and sometimes influence marriages, patronage, succession, or diplomacy. Their visibility should not be mistaken for equality among all women. Court sources illuminate titled women unevenly and say much less about farmers, servants, artisans, captives, and widows.

Clothing communicated wealth, occupation, gender, age, and connection through fabric, cut, color, and ornament. Images and surviving textiles overrepresent elites, while children often appear dressed like smaller adults. One luxurious robe cannot set the weekday wardrobe for an oil worker, shepherd, fisher, or baker.

Seljuq-era objects reveal cups, lamps, bowls, textiles, writing tools, jewelry, and furnishings used in varied settings. Their beauty often reflects court or prosperous households. Ordinary homes probably mixed local pottery, wood, basketry, cloth, repaired tools, and precious items, but exact Shirvan room inventories are absent.

Households could include relatives, dependents, servants, apprentices, guests, and enslaved people, with sharply unequal freedom and security. Islamic legal and devotional objects illuminate ideals more clearly than private affection. Family life involved care and celebration alongside work, hierarchy, illness, bereavement, and sometimes coercion.

Children learned speech, prayer, manners, chores, crafts, routes, songs, and social rank by watching and participating. Wealthy families might hire tutors, while artisans trained apprentices. No Shirvan attendance register survives, so childhood education belongs in homes, workshops, mosques, courts, and streets rather than one imaginary schoolhouse.

Mosques and teachers could provide Quran recitation, hadith, law, and Arabic grammar; madrasas developed unevenly across the Islamic world. Medicine, philosophy, literature, and practical skills were also taught in homes or scholarly circles. No source proves that every Shirvan child attended a formal school.

Early New Persian used Arabic script and expanded as a language of literature, administration, and scholarship under Turkic dynasties including the Seljuqs. Shirvan's court participated in that Persian literary world. Regional speech remained more diverse than the surviving elite texts, which strongly favor educated writers.

Arabic remained central to religion and scholarship while Persian absorbed Arabic vocabulary and writing conventions. Bilingual poets and officials moved between languages. Caucasian and Turkic languages were also present regionally, yet the archive does not provide a tidy household language survey for Shamakhi or Baku.

Written-language sample: فلک کژروتر است از خط ترسا. Transliteration: Falak kazh-rawtar ast az khatt-e tarsa. Translation: the heavens are more crooked than a Christian's script. This short Persian line opens a famous poem by Khaqani; it represents elite literature, not everyone's everyday conversation.

Khaqani's own poems describe a complex education involving his learned uncle, court patrons, travel, family loss, confinement, and intellectual ambition. Poetry can preserve lived emotion and precise names, but stylized praise and complaint require interpretation. His brilliant voice is evidence, not Shirvan's universal diary.

sections.title: Hear poetry, worship, celebrate, and remember

items.text: Court poets praised rulers, requested rewards, competed, complained, and displayed encyclopedic learning. Their verses reveal titles, places, patrons, ceremonies, and expectations while using deliberate exaggeration. A king compared to the sun probably brightened a poem more reliably than he improved the weather.

Shirvan and Georgian courts exchanged people, stories, music, feasting customs, and Persian literary forms amid warfare and alliance. Khaqani even used Georgian material. Cultural borrowing did not erase religious or political difference; neighbors could admire a song, arrange a marriage, and still dispute a fortress.

Seljuq-period art joined Arabic calligraphy, Persian literary culture, geometric design, animals, plants, and princely scenes across ceramics, metalwork, textiles, and manuscripts. Objects traveled and styles were adapted locally. A motif found in Shirvan might signal fashion or trade rather than direct imperial ownership.

Quran manuscripts, mosque furnishings, and funerary art show devotion expressed through skilled materials and writing. Religious life also included prayer, fasting, charity, teaching, pilgrimage, local shrines, and family remembrance. Surviving luxury objects should not crowd ordinary worshippers out of the story.

Baku's preserved monuments embody many later building campaigns and restorations. They help children see how cities remember rulers, but most famous palace structures postdate this card. Archaeology, inscriptions, and fabric analysis must date each feature before it becomes evidence for twelfth-century worship or court ceremony.

sections.title: Treat illness and manage water, waste, and toilets

items.text: Akhawayni's tenth-century Persian medical compendium proves that learned medicine circulated in a language increasingly used for science. Physicians inherited Greek, Arabic, Iranian, and practical traditions, but no surviving Shirvan clinic register names local patients. Scholarly medicine existed; universal access and cure rates did not.

Bimaristans elsewhere in the Islamic world combined treatment, teaching, staff, medicines, and careful access to water, usually in major cities. No secure evidence places such a hospital in this card's Shirvan. Most care likely happened through households, local practitioners, midwives, pharmacists, and religious support.

Medical learning drew on authors such as Galen, Dioscorides, al-Razi, and Ibn Sina, using observation, compound drugs, diet, and inherited theory. Manuscripts and instruments belonged especially to trained practitioners. A learned prescription should not be confused with what every sick shepherd, sailor, or child could obtain.

Bathhouses in regional cities supported washing, ritual purity, warmth, grooming, treatment, and sociability through furnaces, water carriers, attendants, and scheduled access. Evidence does not prove one in every Shirvan settlement. A hammam was infrastructure and workplace, not merely a luxurious medieval bubble bath.

No securely identified universal household toilet or sewer system survives for Shirvan. People likely used pits, vessels, courtyards, drains, middens, and designated outdoor places according to setting and wealth. Comparative latrines preserve parasite eggs spectacularly; regrettably, germs never respected royal titles or polite silence.

Shirvan's achievement was resilient connection: rulers, port workers, farmers, craftspeople, scholars, sailors, and merchants linked the Caucasus with Caspian and Iranian networks despite raids and overlords. Baku's oil, salt, saffron, silk, carpets, fishing, shipping, and customs supported wealth, though surviving quantities often come from later reports.

The Shamakhi court helped sustain one of the great Persian poets. Khaqani transformed politics, theology, science, grief, travel, and rivalry into demanding verse that outlived his patrons. The achievement belongs also to teachers, scribes, paper makers, readers, and performers who allowed poetry to circulate.

Historical and seismological studies report a severe Shamakhi earthquake around 1191 or 1192, but casualty figures and immediate political consequences are uncertain. Earthquake risk shaped rebuilding and memory over centuries. One dramatic shock should not become a convenient explanation for every damaged wall or royal move.

At 1200 the atlas removes exact id shirvan and repaints sampled places under other broad labels, including an implausible return of Buwayhid coloring. This is a database seam, not documented conquest. The geometry audit exposes the handoff so children do not mistake a cartographic glitch for mass evacuation.

The Shirvanshah tradition continued beyond 1200 through changing branches, tributary relationships, Mongol pressure, and later capitals. Families, farms, ports, poems, religious communities, and unpleasant chores also crossed the software boundary. History rarely pauses just because a dropdown menu needs the next century.

ending.text: No Shirvanshah state fell in one securely dated event in 1200. The dynasty began before the atlas interval and continued afterward through contested branches, tribute, warfare, and changing centers. Coins, court poetry, and neighboring histories show political transformation rather than an empty landscape. The exact map feature disappears between the 1100 and 1200 snapshots, while the later snapshot oddly assigns sampled Shamakhi, Baku, Qabala, and surrounding points to a broad Buwayhid layer. That cartographic repaint cannot document conquest, extinction, or evacuation. This card therefore ends with continuity and an explicit software handoff. It leaves successors empty because no single exact id inherits the whole polity at that date. Farmers, fishers, merchants, craftspeople, scholars, rulers, children, patients, bath workers, and families kept living amid later powers, and the Shirvanshah name remained politically important for centuries.
